performers: John Harrison, violin; Wichita State University Chamber Players; Robert Turizziani, conductor
intro: Nymphs and shepherds dance to lilting violins over the long E and B of a country bagpipe. Vivaldi lets the dance wander into C♯ minor and E minor before bringing everyone home.

sections.label: A · The bagpipe dance
sections.mNote: A lilting violin tune above long E and B notes

sections.label: B · The soloist leaves the drone
sections.mNote: Rising sequences and a chromatic bass lead towards C♯ minor

sections.label: A′ · The dance in C♯ minor
sections.mNote: The refrain returns in C♯ minor and reaches B major

sections.label: C · Solo violin and answering strings
sections.mNote: The solo travels through several keys above sustained bass notes

sections.label: A″ · The dance turns to E minor
sections.mNote: The refrain begins in E major, then loses its G♯

sections.label: D · Solo violin over B
sections.mNote: The bass holds B while the upper strings rest

sections.label: A · The last E-major dance
sections.mNote: The full strings return to E major

cues.title: A country bagpipe
cues.text: “Di pastoral Zampogna al Suon festante” — “To the merry sound of a shepherd’s bagpipe.” The 1725 sonnet gives this dance its instrument. Long E and B notes in the bass imitate the bagpipe’s drone while the violin tune rocks in four groups of three quavers.
cues.evidence: Spring sonnet, letter G; translation ours. Mutopia score after Performers’ Facsimiles, III, bars 1–12, marked Danza Pastorale in 12/8: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=301.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The dance in C♯ minor
cues.text: The strings return with the same rocking dance in C♯ minor. The bass holds C♯ where it first held E. Soon it starts moving again, carrying the tune through E major towards B major.
cues.evidence: Mutopia score, III, bars 22–34; José Rodríguez Alvira traces the progression: https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2021/vivaldi-seasons/primavera/03.php.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Nymphs beside the shepherds
cues.text: “Danzan Ninfe e Pastor nel tetto amato / Di primavera all’apparir brillante” — “Nymphs and shepherds dance beneath their beloved shelter at spring’s brilliant arrival.” The sonnet puts mythological nymphs beside working shepherds. Their music is the same country dance.
cues.evidence: Spring sonnet, 1725, final two lines, letter G; translation ours. The text is printed with the Mutopia score and reproduced at https://nac-cna.ca/en/event/notes/36996. The sonnets were published anonymously.

cues.title: G♯ becomes G♮
cues.text: The dance returns in E major, then turns to E minor. G♯ becomes G♮; the bass descends by semitones beneath the familiar lilt. The tune keeps dancing through the change.
cues.evidence: Mutopia score, III, bars 58–70, including the change to E minor in bar 61 and chromatic bass descent; commentary at https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2021/vivaldi-seasons/primavera/03.php.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Back to the bagpipe
cues.text: The long bass B resolves to E, and the full strings restore the major-key dance. The final phrase has a soft echo. After the soloist’s wandering, the bass can settle back into its bagpipe drone.
cues.evidence: Mutopia score, III, bars 79–89, with the return to E major and the later piano echo: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=301.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The drone starts walking
transitions.to: B · The soloist leaves the drone
transitions.how: The solo violin leaves the full-string dance while the bass still holds E. Then the bass begins to move: ascending sequences pass through A and B towards C♯ minor. A descent by semitones tightens the approach to the next refrain.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia score, III, bars 12–22; bass and harmonic route shown at https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2021/vivaldi-seasons/primavera/03.php.

transitions.title: The strings land on C♯
transitions.from: B · The soloist leaves the drone
transitions.to: A′ · The dance in C♯ minor
transitions.how: The bass resolves G♯ to C♯. The full strings resume the opening dance in C♯ minor over a long C♯ pedal. Its dotted rhythm survives intact, then a descending-fifths progression takes the phrase through E major towards B major.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia score, III, bars 21–34; harmonic sequence explained at https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2021/vivaldi-seasons/primavera/03.php.

transitions.title: B major releases the soloist
transitions.from: A′ · The dance in C♯ minor
transitions.to: C · Solo violin and answering strings
transitions.how: The bass moves E–F♯–B at the cadence. The soloist begins a new episode in B major while short bass notes punctuate the phrase. A chain of fifths carries it through E, A and D before the music finds its way back to B.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia score, III, bars 33–58; key sequence in Rodríguez Alvira’s commentary: https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2021/vivaldi-seasons/primavera/03.php.

transitions.title: The returning dance loses G♯
transitions.from: C · Solo violin and answering strings
transitions.to: A″ · The dance turns to E minor
transitions.how: The solo episode ends in B major. The bass restores its long E and the strings begin the dance in E major. At bar 61 the key signature changes to one sharp: G♮ replaces G♯, and the refrain continues in E minor.

transitions.title: A long B under the solo
transitions.from: A″ · The dance turns to E minor
transitions.how: The bass descends E–D♯–D–C♯–C–B and holds the B. The orchestral violins withdraw, leaving the soloist above that dominant pedal. The held note lasts through the episode until the final return to E major.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia score, III, bars 68–79, bass descent and sustained B: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=301.

transitions.title: E major after the long B
transitions.how: The bass leaves its long B for E, and the full strings resume the dance in E major. The soloist rejoins the orchestral violins. Long E and B notes support the last phrases, including their piano echo.

source.title: Vivaldi, The Four Seasons — Mutopia score after Performers’ Facsimiles
source.locator: III. Allegro, especially bars 1–14, 22, 34–58, 71–89. Passage-level participation, not individual attack alignment; cellos/basses represent the written basso part, with no claim about keyboard realization.

timeline.note: Full-string dance over sustained bass notes.
First solo episode; orchestral upper strings rest while the basso supports the violin.
The minor-key refrain restores the full strings.
Extended solo-led passage; upper strings answer and the bass later rests, so this is passage-level participation.
The refrain returns and changes from E major to E minor.
Solo violin over the sustained B bass; orchestral violins rest.
The full-string closing dance regains E major.

composer.epithet: He wrote concertos for the women of Venice’s Pietà, operas for its theatres, and a barking dog for the viola.
facts: Violin with his father Giovanni Battista, a player at St Mark’s, Venice
Pietà violin teacher from 1703; maestro de’ concerti from 1716; court service in Mantua, 1718–20
More than 500 concertos, operas, sacred music and sonatas
composer.background:
In 1703 a twenty-five-year-old Venetian became a priest in March and a violin teacher in September. Antonio Vivaldi had red hair, a formidable bow arm and a chest complaint that made celebrating Mass difficult. His father Giovanni Battista had been a barber before joining the violinists at St Mark’s; he taught Antonio and continued helping with his career long after the son had become famous. Venice knew Antonio as il prete rosso, the red priest. His working places would be the chapel, the orchestra gallery and the opera house.

The Ospedale della Pietà cared for abandoned children. Its musical establishment was a selected group of girls and women, trained to sing and play to a standard that brought visitors from across Europe. Some remained there as adult musicians and teachers. Vivaldi taught the advanced string players, rehearsed the orchestra and supplied new pieces. The governors voted on his employment each year: in 1709 they dispensed with him, and in 1711 took him back. The music survived the office politics.
